title: Finding customers for Lindus
lede: Lindus stopped selling trials in August 2026 and now buys drug assets, so the "customer" to win is a biotech that owns a chronic-disease drug and can't fund the next trial alone.

company.name: Lindus Therapeutics
company.one_liner: Next-generation drug developer that in-licenses clinical-stage assets and runs the trials itself.

glossary.ICP: Ideal customer profile: the kind of company that buys, and why. For Lindus, the kind of company that would hand over a drug asset.
glossary.persona: A specific person inside the target company, described by role, what they own and why they would care.
glossary.buying signal: Something you can see from outside that makes the need urgent now, like a readout, a funding gap or a pivot.
glossary.licensor: The company that owns a drug asset and grants the rights to develop it to someone else. Lindus's real customer.
glossary.in-licensing: Taking the rights to someone else's drug asset, usually for an upfront fee, milestones and royalties.
glossary.CVR: Contingent value right: a promise to pay former shareholders if an asset later earns money, often used when a company plans to sell an asset.
glossary.ex-APAC rights: The rights to a drug everywhere except Asia-Pacific, the deal type an Asian drug owner offers a Western partner.
glossary.champion: The person inside the account who wants the deal and pushes it internally.
glossary.economic buyer: The person who can say yes and sign. In a small biotech that is usually the CEO with the board.

lessons.title: Who buys this?
lessons.idea: Lindus used to sell trials. Since August 2026 it does {{in-licensing}} of drug assets, so the company you have to win is the one that owns the drug and decides who develops it next.

blocks.body: Curavit bought the CRO assets of Lindus Health on 18 August 2026, and Lindus now calls itself Lindus Therapeutics [s4, s6]. The home page says it in-licenses "phase I-III ready assets" in "non-ultrarare chronic disease" and funds the first deals from its own balance sheet [s1]. So the old buyer, a trial sponsor, is now someone else's customer.

blocks.heading: Where Lindus has proof it can run trials
blocks.caption: The 14 sponsor trials Lindus announced on its own news page, by area [s2]. Only 3 were drug trials; most were devices and digital therapeutics.

blocks.name: Beachhead market
blocks.body: For Lindus the beachhead is small Western biotechs with a Phase 2-ready chronic-disease drug and not enough cash for the next trial. They have the most reason to take a partner that runs the trial, and they match every line of Lindus's own brief [s1, s3]. Asian owners offering {{ex-APAC rights}} are the second lane, not the first.

blocks.title: The decision, and why
blocks.body: Four segments were on the table: old trial sponsors, big pharma pruning its pipeline, small biotechs short of cash, and Asian drug owners. Sponsors went to Curavit with the CRO [s4], and big pharma runs auctions that an $80M balance sheet rarely wins (our judgement). Small biotechs fit Lindus's stated rule of "in-licensing programs after early clinical readouts" [s3], so they come first.

items.label: Who
items.value: Clinical-stage biotechs (and some pharma) that own a drug with human data, typically Phase 2-ready [s1]

items.label: Disease areas
items.value: Non-ultrarare chronic disease where Lindus has run trials: cardiometabolic, respiratory, psychiatry, dermatology, women's health [s1, s2]

items.label: Size
items.value: Small caps and venture-backed privates with roughly a year of cash or less, or a pivot away from the asset

items.label: Regions
items.value: Owner anywhere; the trial runs in the US, UK and Europe [s1]

items.label: The pain, in their words
items.value: "Subject to receipt of additional financing" [s14]; "to be divested or partnered" [s17]

items.label: Not a fit
items.value: Acquired or being acquired; cash-rich and running its own next trial; rare disease or oncology; bankrupt; no human data

items.label: Why now
items.value: Lindus is targeting deal close on its first assets through 2026 [s1]

blocks.heading: The {{persona}} cards: who is in a licensing deal

items.title: CEO
items.body: Owns the runway and the story to investors. Cares whether a deal funds the next value step without a dilutive raise.

items.title: Chief Business Officer or head of BD
items.body: Runs the partnering process and the data room. Cares about a credible partner who can close fast.

items.title: Chief Medical Officer
items.body: Judges whether Lindus can run the next trial well. Cares about enrollment speed and data quality, where Lindus has a record [s1].

items.title: Board and lead investor
items.body: Want value from the asset. Often push for a partner when cash is short.

blocks.title: Your own website is trap number one
blocks.body: The home page says Lindus Therapeutics with a team of 80 [s1], but the leadership page still says "Lindus is a next-generation CRO" and "Over 160 people" [s7]. A biotech CEO who clicks through will wonder which company is writing to them. Fix or redirect the old pages before any outreach.

quiz.q: A small biotech's CMO loves how Lindus runs trials. Who most likely signs the licence?
options: The CMO
The CEO, with the board
The head of clinical operations
The lead investigator at the trial site
quiz.why: In a small biotech the CEO and board own the runway and the asset, so they sign. The CMO is the one who can block it on trial quality.

quiz.q: Which company is outside the beachhead?
options: A Swedish biotech with Phase 2a obesity data and one funded trial
A US biotech with a positive Phase 2 in asthma and a year of cash
A trial sponsor that used Lindus as its CRO in 2024 and wants another trial run
A biotech shelving a Phase 3 acne drug after a pivot
quiz.why: Running trials for sponsors is now Curavit's business [s4]. The other three own assets and have a reason to take a partner.

lessons.title: Where are they?
lessons.idea: A target list is only useful if every row is a company that could actually hand Lindus an asset this year. Most wrong rows come from a few traps you can check for.

stages.label: Fit the ICP on the facts

items.label: Cash-rich, running its own next trial

blocks.name: Tier your accounts
blocks.body: Not every licensor deserves a letter this week. A fresh readout plus a short runway, like Connect's, gets a personal note now; a good asset with no trigger, like Gesynta's, goes on the watch list. The matrix below places each account only on dated evidence.

blocks.caption: Checked 24 September 2026. "Bot wall" means the site blocked automated fetches; the company was confirmed through its own investor releases.

blocks.title: Acquired while you were researching
blocks.body: Terns had put its obesity assets up for partnering [s40], which looks like a perfect lead. Then Merck completed its acquisition of Terns on 5 May 2026 [s41]. AtaiBeckley, the former employer of Lindus's own VP of Corporate Development, is now part of Lilly too [s42].

blocks.title: A new name, and a lookalike domain
blocks.body: VYNE Therapeutics merged into Yarrow Bioscience, and vynetherapeutics.com now redirects to yarrowbioscience.com [s28]. yarrowbio.com is a different, empty "Coming Soon" site [s58]. Put the redirecting domain in the table, not the one a search suggests.

blocks.title: A competitor is already in
blocks.body: Sciwind licensed the oral version of its GLP-1 outside China to Verdiva Bio [s29], a company that also builds a pipeline by licensing assets. Only the injectable's rights abroad are still open [s31, s32]. Pitch the asset that is actually available.

blocks.title: Closed, and the assets belong to someone else
blocks.body: Mithra's menopause drug fits the women's health brief perfectly. But Mithra went bankrupt in 2024 and Gedeon Richter owns its estetrol assets [s43]. Old directories still list Mithra as a developer.

blocks.title: Rich companies don't need you
blocks.body: Upstream Bio has $261M and is starting its own Phase 3s [s44]; Altimmune has $535M [s45]. A great asset with a funded owner is not a lead. Six of the 15 drops were this.

blocks.heading: The checks, in order
items: Open the domain. Confirm name, drug and location match; follow redirects and note renames.
Search "<company> acquired" and "<company> merger", newest first. Drop anything bought or being bought.
Check it is still operating: a filing, results release or trial update from the last 90 days.
Read the latest quarterly release for cash runway and who funds the next trial.
Check the asset's rights: who already holds China, Asia or global rights?
Confirm the disease area is chronic and not rare, and that the drug has human data.
If any check can't be settled, drop the row and write down why.

quiz.q: Two sites come up for "Yarrow": yarrowbio.com and yarrowbioscience.com. Which check settles which one is the ex-VYNE company?
options: Pick the shorter domain
Open the old company's domain and see where it redirects
Search the CEO's name
Pick the one with more pages
quiz.why: vynetherapeutics.com redirects to yarrowbioscience.com [s28]. The other domain is an unrelated empty page [s58].

quiz.q: A biotech has a great Phase 2 obesity asset and $400M in the bank. Where does it go?
options: Write now
Watch list or drop: funded owners rarely license out
Top of the list: big budgets mean big deals
Hand it to the agent
quiz.why: Lindus needs owners who can't or won't fund the next trial. Cash-rich owners run it themselves, like Upstream Bio [s44].

lessons.title: When are they ready?
lessons.idea: The same biotech says no in March and yes in September. A {{buying signal}} is a public event that makes the owner need a partner now: fresh data, a funding gap, a pivot.

blocks.name: Trigger events
blocks.body: Lindus says it in-licenses "after early clinical readouts" [s3], which is itself the trigger. A readout raises the asset's value while the owner's cash stays the same. Write in the week of the readout, not the week you finished your list.

items.name: Asset put up for sale or partnering
items.watch: "Divest", "strategic alternatives", a CVR tied to one asset, or a pivot away from a disease area in a release or 8-K
items.why: The owner has already decided not to fund the asset. The only question is who takes it.

example.fact: Nimacimab to be divested or partnered, with proceeds to former holders via a {{CVR}} [s17]

items.name: Early readout, thin runway
items.watch: A Phase 1b or 2 topline release in the same quarter as a runway of about a year or less
items.why: The asset just got more valuable and the next trial just got more expensive. That is when a trial-running partner looks best.

example.fact: Positive Phase 2 in acute asthma; $31.5M cash, about one year of runway [s38, s39]

items.name: Next trial "subject to financing"
items.watch: That phrase, or "pending additional capital", in a quarterly release or 10-Q
items.why: They are telling investors they can't start without new money. A partner is the alternative to a dilutive raise.

example.fact: RECOVER-2 enrollment pushed to H1 2027, subject to additional financing [s14]

items.name: New business development leader
items.watch: Appointment of a Chief Business or Corporate Development Officer
items.why: A new BD chief builds a partner list in the first 90 days.

example.fact: Appointed a Chief Corporate Development Officer with licensing experience [s20]

items.name: Asian owner seeking a partner outside Asia
items.watch: Local business press or English releases about licensing rights outside China or Korea
items.why: This is the {{ex-APAC rights}} deal Lindus lists on its own site [s1].

example.fact: CEO says the aim is a licensing deal for DD01 by year-end [s34]

blocks.title: Signals go stale
blocks.body: Most of these are worth acting on for 30 to 90 days. Vistagen's BD hire is already 101 days old today, so lead with its June Phase 3 news instead, or wait for the next trigger. D&D's is different: it lasts until they sign someone.

quiz.q: Which of these is a buying signal for Lindus, not just news?
options: Lilly completes its acquisition of AtaiBeckley
Connect Biopharma reports a positive Phase 2 with a year of cash left
A trade body publishes a women's health funding report
quiz.why: A fresh readout plus a short runway is the moment a trial-running partner matters. An acquisition closes the door; a report is context.

lessons.title: Who exactly?
lessons.idea: Write to the person who runs partnering, then bring in the person who signs. In small biotechs people leave after every failed trial, so check they are still there first.

blocks.name: Champion vs economic buyer
blocks.body: The {{champion}} at a licensor is the head of BD, who wants a deal done. The {{economic buyer}} is the CEO with the board, who decides whether giving up rights beats raising money. Win the first with speed and a clean term sheet; win the second with a trial plan and a timeline.

blocks.heading: The roles to reach
rows: Chief Business Officer / head of BD
A credible partner that can close before cash runs out
Leadership page; named in deal and partnering releases; conference partnering lists
Funding the next step without a dilutive raise
Quarterly results release (quoted by name); annual report
Whether Lindus can run the next trial fast and clean
Leadership page; trial registry entries; conference posters
Proxy filing; the investor's portfolio page
A Western partner with trial capacity in the US and Europe
English-language releases; US subsidiary team page

blocks.heading: Check a person still works there
items: Find them on the company's own leadership page today, not in an old release.
Check their public profile lists this company as current, with the same domain.
Look for something recent: quoted in a release, a conference talk, or a post in the last 90 days.
After a failed trial or a merger, check again: teams change fast (Neumora cut 35% of staff in June [s49]).
Write to two people per account: BD and the CEO or CMO.

blocks.title: The faster version
blocks.body: Otto can find and verify the people in each role at your 15 accounts, checked against their current employer.

blocks.title: Check one person
blocks.body: Pick Connect Biopharma. Find the person who runs business development and the CEO on its own site, then confirm both still list Connect as their current employer. Note the date you checked.

lessons.title: What do you say?
lessons.idea: The first message is about their asset and their problem, not about Lindus. Prove you read their news, make one point, ask one easy question.

blocks.name: Problem before product
blocks.body: A biotech CEO gets pitched by CROs and bankers every week. What they have not heard is someone who read last week's readout and last quarter's cash line and put the two together. Lead with that, and let Lindus's record come up in the reply.

left.label: The message everyone sends
left.body: Hi Sam, hope you're well! I'm reaching out from Lindus Therapeutics, a next-generation drug development company backed by Peter Thiel. We pair proprietary AI asset selection with an integrated trial platform to reach value inflection points faster. Would you be open to a quick 30-minute call next week to explore potential synergies?

right.label: Yours, to Connect Biopharma
right.body:
Hi [first name], saw Seabreeze STAT cut treatment failure by 66% in acute asthma, with the COPD readout due this month.

The next step is a Phase 3, and the last quarterly report showed $31.5M in cash.

Is that Phase 3 something you plan to fund alone, or would you look at a partner who runs the trial and shares the upside?
right.notes: Opens on their 15 September readout [s38] and their own cash figure [s39]. One either/or question they can answer from memory. No call ask, no investor names, no "AI".

blocks.heading: The rules applied
items: Open on their signal, with a number from their own release.
Say why it matters from their side in one sentence.
Ask one either/or question.
Under 90 words; no meeting ask, no hype words.
Send in the signal's window: this one is fresh until mid-December.

quiz.q: Which opening line gets a reply from a biotech CEO?
options: "Hope you're well! Lindus is a next-generation drug developer."
"We're backed by Peter Thiel and Bob Langer."
"Saw the Phase 2 cut treatment failure by 66%; the Phase 3 is next."
quiz.why: It is about them, it is specific, and it shows you read their news. The other two are about Lindus.

lessons.title: Which Claude model for which job?
lessons.idea: Sorting and extracting at volume doesn't need the biggest model; judgement calls do. We measured it on this course's own accounts.

blocks.name: Match the tool to the job
blocks.body: Lindus will screen hundreds of assets to sign four or five. Screening is volume work; the final call on a licence is expensive to get wrong. Use the cheapest model that sorts well, and the best one where a mistake costs a deal.

blocks.takeaway: All three models caught every disqualifier: the Merck buyout, the bankruptcy, the cash-rich companies and the rare-disease focus. Haiku lost two real fits because it read "program paused" and "funded but seeking partners" as reasons to walk away, which is backwards for an in-licenser. Sonnet and Opus only disagreed with our key on Corbus, and they have a point: the line shows a fresh readout but no stated cash gap or partner search, so our "fit" was a timing judgement. Sonnet matched Opus for about half the price, so it is the default for sorting; use Haiku only as a first pass with a human reading its no-fits.

blocks.body: Total cost of the lab: $0.0721, run on 24 September 2026 with the list prices in model-lab.json (checked the same day) [s57]. Prices change, so re-check before you plan a budget.

lessons.title: Can this run without me?
lessons.idea: Everything in lessons 1 to 5 can run every week. An agent is a model with instructions, tools and a way to check its own work; Claude Managed Agents hosts it on your schedule and grades each run against a rubric.

blocks.name: Systems beat heroics
blocks.body: Readouts and runway warnings land every week across these 15 companies. A Monday check you never skip will catch Connect-style windows that a quarterly push misses. Put the watching on a schedule and spend your time on the calls.

blocks.caption: The kit is in agent/. MODEL is set to Sonnet 5 because it matched Opus in the lab at about half the price.

blocks.title: Cost and control
blocks.body: Each run reads news and filings for 15 companies, so cost grows with the list; each run's cost shows in the Console, and RUN_BUDGET_CENTS in .env is a hard cap per run. The agent only writes a report: it sends nothing and contacts no one. The kit can also connect Otto for verified contacts at each account with a signal.

blocks.title: Keep trial data out of it
blocks.body: Lindus runs clinical trials, which involve patient health data. This agent only reads public web data. Never give it trial, patient or partner data-room files.

quiz.q: The agent's first run flags Terns as "ready" because of its partnering news, but Merck bought Terns in May. What do you change so it doesn't happen again?
options: The instructions
The rubric
The schedule
quiz.why: Add a rubric line that every reported company must still be independent, so the grader sends the run back when it isn't. Instructions help, but only the rubric makes it a checked rule.

lessons.title: What happens next?
lessons.idea: A list and a message are a plan. Pipeline comes from sending, following up, handling replies and learning which assets say yes.

blocks.name: Founder-led sales first
blocks.body: The first five licences will be won by the CEO, the VP of Corporate Development and the CMO in the room, not by a sequence. Only they can change the deal shape, from an option to a co-development to a SpinCo, in the same call [s1]. Automate the watching and the first touch; keep the conversations.

blocks.heading: Setting up a campaign in Otto from this course
items: Bring the accounts in: import the lesson 2 table into a workbook named after this course, with each domain so Otto matches existing companies.
Bring the people in: add the BD heads and CEOs you verified, as a dry run first; every person should attach to one of the 15 companies, with no new companies created.
Pick a sequence: create a draft campaign from a template. Nothing launches yet.
Write the steps: the lesson 5 message as step 1, then one or two follow-ups that each bring a new fact (the COPD readout, a trial timeline), not a repeat.
Enrol and schedule: add the workbook, set send days, window, time zone and a daily cap.
Check before launch: run the pre-launch check for missing leads, empty copy, no connected mailbox or LinkedIn account, or no schedule.
Launch when you're ready, yourself. Replies land in Otto's inbox, sorted, with drafts for your approval.

blocks.title: Nothing sends until you launch it
blocks.body: This course made no campaign and sent nothing. Start at [otto-pilot.io](https://otto-pilot.io) when you want the sending, follow-up and replies handled.

quiz.q: The pre-launch check says "no mailbox that can see replies". What happens if you try to launch anyway?
options: It sends and you miss the replies
Otto refuses to launch until the blocker is fixed
It launches on LinkedIn only
quiz.why: The pre-launch check blocks launch until the missing piece is fixed.
